Maryland man indicted on wire fraud and identity theft charges in gift card scheme
A Randallstown man has been indicted on multiple counts related to an alleged gift-card scam causing over $53,000 in losses across Maryland residents' accounts. Federal authorities detail how stolen credit cards were used illegally while emphasizing all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty.
A Maryland man is facing a federal indictment for his alleged involvement in a gift-card scheme, the U.S. Attorney’s Office announced on Oct. 7.
Sharieff Tate Pierre, 36, of Randallstown, has been charged with 21 counts of wire fraud and 21 counts of aggravated identity theft after allegedly using stolen credit cards to purchase gift cards. According to the indictment, Pierre victimized 21 individuals and caused losses totaling $53,300.49.
The indictment was announced by Kelly O. Hayes, U.S. Attorney for the District of Maryland; Damon E. Wood, Postal Inspector in Charge at the U.S. Postal Inspection Service – Washington Division; Kathleen Woodson, Executive Special Agent in Charge at the U.S. Postal Service Office of Inspector General Mid-Atlantic Area Field Office; and Chief Robert McCullough of the Baltimore County Police Department.
Court documents state that an investigation began in July 2021 after a financial institution reported that some cardholders had not received their credit cards by mail and later discovered unauthorized charges on those accounts. The indictment alleges that Pierre obtained credit cards intended for other individuals from victim institutions and used personal information such as names and dates of birth without lawful authority to buy gift cards. He then allegedly used Western Union to convert the value from these gift cards into cash and also used personally identifiable information to obtain lines of credit for purchasing vehicles without victims’ knowledge.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office stated, “An indictment is not a finding of guilt. Individuals charged by indictment are presumed innocent until proven guilty at a later criminal proceeding.” If convicted, Pierre faces up to 20 years in prison for each count of wire fraud and up to two years for each count of aggravated identity theft; actual sentences may be less than maximum penalties as determined by federal district court judges under sentencing guidelines.
U.S. Attorney Hayes commended law enforcement agencies involved in the investigation and thanked Assistant U.S. Attorneys Elliot Higgins and Colleen Elizabeth McGuinn who are prosecuting the case.
The U.S. Attorney for the District of Maryland serves nearly six million residents across Maryland with over 200 personnel across civil, criminal, and administrative divisions; it prosecutes federal crimes including fraud cases like this one as part of its role within the Department of Justice, according to the official website.
